sections.h2: Who sends and collects property tax bills in Anderson County, Kentucky?
sections.html:
The Anderson County Sheriff's Office collects property tax. It is at 208 S Main St, Lawrenceburg, KY 40342, phone (502) 839-4021, open Monday through Friday from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. Bills go out to owners at the end of September and collection begins October 1. The office says it no longer mails bills to mortgage companies, so an owner whose lender pays from escrow should still confirm that the lender received the bill.

The value on the bill comes from a separate office, the Property Valuation Administrator, which handles assessments and exemptions. The Sheriff's page gives the PVA's number as (502) 839-4061. Anderson County is a Bluegrass-area county of about 25,000 people with Lawrenceburg as its only city, so most owners deal with these same two offices.

sections.h2: Which parts of Anderson County pay through the same offices?
sections.html: Every parcel in the county uses the same Sheriff and PVA, whether it sits in Lawrenceburg or in one of the unincorporated communities such as Alton, Glensboro, McBrayer or Stringtown. The county covers about 202 square miles of the Outer Bluegrass and touches seven other counties: Franklin, Woodford, Mercer, Washington, Nelson, Spencer and Shelby. A homeowner who owns land across a county line receives a separate bill and files separate appeals in each county.

sections.h2: What does the Anderson County tax bill cost if you pay early, on time or late?
sections.html:
The Sheriff's page spells out the schedule, and it follows Kentucky's regular calendar in KRS 134.015. Payment must be received on the stated day. The office accepts check, cash or money order, takes no partial payments, and does not honor postmarks.

Anderson County Sheriff tax collection schedule (andersoncountysheriff.com)
Payment windowResult
October 1 to November 12 percent discount
November 2 to December 31Face value of the bill
January 1 to January 315 percent penalty
February 1 to close of business April 1510 percent penalty plus 10 percent Sheriff's add-on fee
After April 15Bill moves to the County Clerk

Taxes on a Kentucky property are a personal debt of the owner on the assessment date, and the debt stays attached to the parcel as a lien even after a sale. That is why sellers pay the current year's bill at or before closing.

sections.h2: What happens to an Anderson County tax bill after April 15?
sections.html:
All delinquent bills go to the County Clerk at the close of business on April 15. The Sheriff's page says payments there carry a 20 percent County Attorney fee, a 10 percent Clerk fee and interest of 1 percent per month on top of the penalties already added. The debt can also be sold to a third-party buyer in the summer.

The Department of Revenue illustrates the effect with a $1,000 bill. When it reaches the clerk, the face amount, the 10 percent penalty, the Sheriff's add-on and the Sheriff's commission total $1,254 in its example. Paid within five business days, that example costs $1,387.79, and after the county attorney's first notice it reaches $1,611.30. Actual commission rates vary, so the example only shows the direction of the numbers.

  • The clerk must give a tax-sale list to the Department of Revenue.
  • The county attorney mails a 30-day notice and later a second notice.
  • The sale date falls at least 90 and no more than 135 days after the transfer, under KRS 134.128.

sections.h2: How are Anderson County properties assessed, and how do you appeal?
sections.html:
Kentucky assesses real estate as of January 1. The Department of Revenue says the tax roll is open for inspection for thirteen days starting the first Monday in May, with the PVA required to publish notice of the dates in the largest local newspaper.

An owner who disagrees must first hold a conference with the PVA or a deputy. After that conference the owner files an appeal at the County Clerk's office by the close of business on the day after the inspection period ends. The local board of assessment appeals meets 25 to 35 days after inspection closes, for no more than five days. Bring evidence such as the physical description of the land and buildings, insurance policies, construction cost and real estate sales listings, because the department states that an appeal without this kind of documentation is denied.

  • An owner who skips the local board or does not appear cannot carry the appeal further.
  • If bills are prepared before the appeal ends and the final value is higher than the owner claimed, a supplemental bill follows.
  • A paid representative must be an attorney, accountant, licensed broker, appraiser or other recognized professional.

sections.h2: Can Anderson County homeowners get a homestead exemption?
sections.html:
Yes, if the owner is 65 or older or classified as totally disabled. The Sheriff's page tells those owners to call the PVA at (502) 839-4061. The Department of Revenue says the exemption is $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years and is deducted from the home's assessed value before tax is computed, and the amount is adjusted every two years.

Using the state's own illustration, a home assessed at $200,000 would be taxed on $150,900. Proof of age can be a birth certificate, license or passport. A disability claim usually needs yearly renewal unless the owner is a service-connected disabled veteran or has been found permanently disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

sections.h2: What do Anderson County's home values mean for a tax bill?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 survey puts the median value of an owner-occupied home in Anderson County at $225,100, with 77.6 percent of homes owner-occupied and a median household income of $74,488. Median owner costs are $1,391 a month with a mortgage and $411 without one, so a paid-off home still carries a real cost, and property tax is part of it.

The county grew 5.6 percent between April 2020 and July 2025. An owner who bought recently can list the deed price as the value for the next January 1 assessment if nothing about the property has changed, according to the Department of Revenue.

sections.h2: How should you handle unpaid Anderson County tax when you sell?
sections.html:
• Get a payoff figure from the Sheriff's Office before April 15, or from the County Clerk after it.
  • Pay delinquent amounts out of closing proceeds so the title company can record a release of the lien.
  • Give the buyer's agent the in-care-of address that KRS 382.135 requires on the deed for the year's bill.
  • If you are 65 or older, ask the PVA how the exemption will carry to the next owner's bill.

Owners behind on several years who want to sell without making repairs can ask for a written cash offer. The buyer's closing agent subtracts the tax and clerk charges from the price in the same way a traditional closing does.

faqs.q: When are Anderson County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The face amount is due by December 31, and a 2 percent discount applies through November 1. The Sheriff's schedule adds a 5 percent penalty in January and 10 percent plus a 10 percent add-on from February 1.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Anderson County property tax?
faqs.a: Pay at the Sheriff's Office, 208 S Main St in Lawrenceburg, or call (502) 839-4021. After April 15 the bill is paid at the County Clerk instead.
No. The Sheriff's page states that partial payments are not accepted at this time, and postmarks do not count. The full payment has to reach the office by the date for that rate.

faqs.q: How do I challenge my assessment?
faqs.a: Hold a conference with the PVA, then file the appeal at the County Clerk by the close of business the day after the inspection period ends. The local board hears it 25 to 35 days later.

faqs.q: Who qualifies for the homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Homeowners who are at least 65 or totally disabled qualify. Apply with the PVA at (502) 839-4061. The amount is $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years.
